reason: Both quotes re-verified. Marine Department fact sheet: the VTS 'covers all navigable waters of Hong Kong used by sea-going vessels and ferries' and 'Traffic Separation Schemes are implemented in the East Lamma Channel and Tathong Channel'. Examination Guidebook (PDF metadata ModDate 31 Mar 2026): 'There are two traffic separation schemes (TSS) within Hong Kong waters which are adopted by IMO: (a) Tathong Channel (b) East Lamma Channel'. The guidebook also describes the East Lamma Channel as extending 'southeast from Kennedy Town ... to the southwest of Ngan Chau', which is inside HKSAR waters. No IMO Part I or other MRS applies. Mandatory VTS participation under Cap 313A is correctly treated as a VTS duty. Minor point: my fetch of the fact sheet did not show the 2025-12-31 revision date cited in the record, so that date should be re-checked or dropped. This does not affect the status.

MRS only is upheld, with a recommended consistency rule and a citation fix. (1) MASTREP is a genuine statutory mandatory reporting system. Under MO 63 (2019) s.2 it gives effect to 'Regulation 11 of Chapter V of SOLAS'. Section 6(1) applies it to 'a regulated Australian vessel' and 'a foreign vessel from its arrival at its first port in Australia until its departure from its final port in Australia'. Section 7 carries a strict liability penalty of 50 penalty units. Schedule 3 requires AIS position reports, or manual hourly reports if the AIS is off. The MASTREP area is the JRCC Australia SRR (s.4), which contains the TSS. (2) Consistency with SUNDAREP and LOMBOKREP: those schemes bind only Indonesian-flag ships and place no duty at all on foreign ships. MASTREP does bind foreign ships, with penalties, on every domestic leg between Australian ports, and a large share of Cape Leeuwin traffic is on such legs. A consistent project rule is: a national scheme counts as an MRS if it imposes a penal reporting duty on foreign ships in the TSS under defined voyage conditions. SUNDAREP and LOMBOKREP fail this rule; MASTREP passes it. Keep the applicability caveat that foreign ships on through-transit or on the inbound leg before their first Australian port are outside MASTREP. If the coordinator prefers a strict 'applies to all ships' rule, the status becomes Neither confirmed (see point 3), not Unresolved. (3) VTS side (report only): absence is positively supported. The TasPorts instrument (Dec 2025) shows that VTS providers are authorised under 'Marine Order 64 (Vessel Traffic Services) 2022' and 'may only provide vessel traffic services in the geographical areas approved by AMSA'. AMSA's list (14 Nov 2023) is the closed set of authorised providers; its only south-west WA entry is Fremantle. The VTS side could therefore be recorded as positively 'not associated', with a currency caveat that the list dates from 2023. (4) Citation fix: the AMSA 'VTS areas in Australia' page does not mention Marine Order 64. Attribute the MO 64 link to an MO 64 provider instrument or to MO 64 itself.

Same basis as TSS-0158. MO 63 (2019) s.6(1), s.7 and Schedule 3 make MASTREP reporting mandatory, with penalties, for regulated Australian vessels and for foreign vessels between their first and final Australian ports, throughout the JRCC Australia SRR that contains the TSS. This is consistent with the SUNDAREP and LOMBOKREP treatment if the rule is that a national scheme counts as an MRS when it binds foreign ships under defined voyage conditions. Keep the through-transit caveat. VTS side (report only): no authorised provider on the WA south coast; the AMSA list has no Albany or Esperance entry. The MO 64 2022 condition limiting providers to approved areas makes this a positive absence, subject to the list's 2023 date. The same citation fix applies: the AMSA list page does not itself mention MO 64. Unresolved note kept: the TSS position was not re-plotted, but any position off Chatham Island is far from every listed VTS area.

MASTREP basis verified as for TSS-0158 (MO 63 2019 s.6(1), s.7, Schedule 3; SRR area). Bass Strait coastal traffic is mostly on domestic legs, so a significant share of ships using the TSS is bound. VTS side (report only): the TasPorts MO 64 instrument (Dec 2025) defines the Grassy VTS Area as a '6 nautical miles' radius circle at Grassy Harbour and the Lady Barron VTS Area as a '3 nautical miles' radius circle. The Bell Bay and Devonport areas reach north only to about 40 50 S and 40 58 S. None comes near Wilsons Promontory (about 39 S). The Melbourne (Ports Victoria) area chart was not opened by me either. A 'not associated' VTS finding is well supported here but not formally closed for Melbourne. Citation fix as for TSS-0158.

MASTREP basis verified as for TSS-0158. The TSS is inside the Australian SRR wherever it lies in Bass Strait. VTS side (report only): TasPorts VTS areas are small port areas (Grassy 6 nm radius, Lady Barron 3 nm radius, north-coast ports limited to about 40 50 S to 40 58 S). The TSS position was still not plotted, and Melbourne VTS limits were not opened. Positive VTS absence is therefore likely but not demonstrated for this record. Keep the unresolved_issue. Citation fix as for TSS-0158.

Keep the VTS only status; change vts_coverage from 'full' to 'partial', or explicitly define coverage as lanes only. eCFR 2026-09-01 verified. Under s.161.60(a), the VTS area is US waters 'north of a line drawn from Cape Hinchinbrook Light to Schooner Rock Light ... between 146 30 W and 147 20 W'. Under s.161.60(b), the Valdez Arm VTS Special Area is the Valdez Arm TSS. The PWS lanes (s.167.1702, from 60 20.6 N) and the Valdez Arm TSS lie inside. However, s.167.1700 states that the IMO-adopted scheme 'consists of four parts', including 'two precautionary areas'. The Cape Hinchinbrook precautionary area (s.167.1701(a)) runs to 59 51.80 N and 146 00.01 W. That is south of the VTS line and east of 146 30 W, so a large part of it is outside the VTS area. The Table 161.12(c)(9) VMRS area (north of 60 N, west of 146 30 W) also excludes part of it. The record itself notes this, so coverage 'full' overstates the position for the scheme as a whole.

Keep VTS only, but set vts_coverage to 'partial' for statutory coverage and state the basis explicitly. Quotes verified. RAMN s.3.5.4: 'The CVTS Area of Operation is defined as 124 40W south along the Washington coast to 48 00N then west to 125 15W and north to 48 35'45"N'. Inbound vessels 'check in with Prince Rupert Traffic ... prior to entering the traffic separation scheme'. 'Participation ... is mandatory within Canadian and United States territorial waters.' Table 161.12(c)(10)(iii) gives Prince Rupert Traffic the box to 125 15 W and 48 00 N. Against this, s.161.55(a) defines the CVTS with a western limit on the rhumb line from 48 35.749 N 124 47.5 W to 48 23.5 N 124 48.616 W. The western approach (125 04.67 to 125 09 W) is entirely west of that line. Table note 4 also states: 'Some monitoring areas extend beyond navigable waters. Although not required, users are strongly encouraged to maintain a listening watch'. So the US regulation treats the offshore part of the box as a voluntary monitoring area, not a VTS area. Statutory coverage: SOR/2025-275 (registered 12 Dec 2025, in force three months after publication in CG II of 31 Dec 2025) bounds the Prince Rupert VTS Zone from 48 28 36 N 124 40 W 'following the territorial sea boundary northward'. By my approximate plot, Pachena Point (48 43 20 N 125 05 51 W, named in SOR/2025-275) is about 11.2 nm from the northern edge of the westbound lane (48 32.09 N). The northernmost strip of the westbound lane, roughly north of 48 31.3 N, is therefore probably inside the Canadian territorial sea and so inside the statutory Prince Rupert VTS Zone. This assumes normal baselines; verify on the chart. The rest of the component is covered only by the voluntary CVTS operating area. The two official sources, CCG RAMN and the US Table, both place the whole TSS in Prince Rupert Traffic's service or monitoring area, and RAMN ties check-in to the TSS itself. This meets association standard 3 for a VTS service area, so VTS only (partial) is preferable to Unresolved. If the project requires a statutory VTS area, the result is VTS only with a small partial overlap, and should not be downgraded further.

Keep VTS only, but set vts_coverage to 'partial'. The evidence is as for TSS-0163: the RAMN CVTS Area of Operation and the Table 161.12(c)(10)(iii) Prince Rupert Traffic box contain the component. It lies wholly west of the s.161.55(a) CVTS western limit (about 124 48 W), and Table note 4 makes the watch beyond navigable waters voluntary. Statutory overlap: the VTS Puget Sound area (s.161.55) runs 'due west' from Tatoosh (48 23.5 N) to the US territorial sea boundary and then north along it. By my approximate plot, the north-eastern corner of the north-eastbound lane (48 26.64 N 125 00.81 W) is about 11.5 nm from Cape Flattery Light, 48 23.5 N 124 44.2 W. That corner is inside the US territorial sea and so inside the statutory VTS area. The separation zone corners (48 27.63 N 125 03.38 W, about 13.3 nm) and the south-western parts are outside it. Only a small sliver is statutory VTS; the rest is voluntary CVTS operating area. Recommend VTS only (partial), with the basis 'CVTS operating/monitoring area (voluntary beyond territorial sea); statutory VTS Puget Sound covers only the NE tip'.

Verified. The western lanes (s.167.1311) run from 125 00 W to 123 31.98 W. East of about 124 48 W they are inside the s.161.55(a) CVTS, which covers 'all navigable waters of the Salish Sea', with the rhumb line near 124 48 W as its western limit; Prince Rupert, Vancouver and Seattle centres 'manage traffic within the CVTS area irrespective of the International Boundary'. West of that, by approximate plot, the US half is within about 10 to 11.5 nm of Tatoosh, which puts it in the statutory VTS Puget Sound area. The Canadian half is within about 10 nm of Vancouver Island (coast near 48 42 N at 125 00 W, per the SOR/2025-275 shoreline points). That puts it in the Prince Rupert VTS Zone, which is bounded seaward by the territorial sea from 48 28 36 N 124 40 W. SOR/2025-275 is in force: it was published in CG II on 31 Dec 2025 and s.40 brings it into force three months after publication. Status and full coverage upheld. The coordinator's CVTS entity question remains open.
